# Target
The compiled C++ binary is /workspace/dataset/test5_executable .
Its source (the test driver only) is /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp :

    if (argc < 2) return 1;
    std::string url = argv[1];
    url_parser::URL parser(url);
    std::cout << parser.scheme() << std::endl;   // line 1
    std::cout << parser.host()   << std::endl;   // line 2
    std::cout << parser.port()   << std::endl;   // line 3  (an integer; -1 when absent)
    std::cout << parser.path()   << std::endl;   // line 4
    std::cout << parser.query()  << std::endl;   // line 5

So EVERY successful run prints exactly 5 newline-terminated lines. Empty fields print as empty lines.
The library source is NOT available and you must NOT try to find or read it. Pure black-box probing.

# How to probe (IMPORTANT)
Run it like:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'THE_URL'
To see exact bytes including empty trailing lines, ALWAYS capture with a delimiter, e.g.:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | sed -n 'l' ; echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
or the most reliable formatting for reporting — number every line:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | cat -A | nl -ba
Use single quotes around the URL. For URLs containing single quotes, control characters, or
non-UTF8 bytes, use perl to exec with an exact argv, e.g.:
    perl -e 'exec("/workspace/dataset/test5_executable", "http://a\x27b.com")' | cat -A | nl -ba
Batch many probes in ONE bash call with a loop so you use few tool calls, e.g.:
    for u in 'http://a' 'http://a:1' 'a://b'; do printf '=== [%s]\n' "$u"; /workspace/dataset/test5_executable "$u" | cat -A | nl -ba; done
`cat -A` renders end-of-line as `$`, tabs as `^I`, so an empty field shows as a line containing only `$`.
Probe generously — dozens to hundreds of inputs. It is cheap. Note python3 is NOT installed; perl is.
Do not write anything into /workspace/dataset or /output. Use /tmp for scratch files.

# What to report
Report the OBSERVED FACTS, not guesses. For each rule you state, cite at least one concrete
input and its exact 5 field values. If two plausible rules both explain your data, say so and
design a discriminating probe, then run it. Be exhaustive within your assigned dimension.


Below is a CANDIDATE SPECIFICATION of the parser, synthesized from earlier probes. Your job is
adversarial: find inputs where the candidate spec predicts something DIFFERENT from what the real
binary actually does. Focus your attack on this lens: IPv6 bracket hosts, userinfo with embedded ":" and "@", and multibyte/high-bit bytes.

Method: read the spec, mentally execute it on candidate inputs, PREDICT the 5 outputs, then run the
real binary and compare. Report only inputs where prediction != reality (plus the corrected
behaviour), and any input where the spec is silent/ambiguous so you cannot predict at all.
Try at least 60 distinct inputs in your lens. Batch them in few bash calls.

CANDIDATE SPEC pseudocode:
========================================================================
REFERENCE SPEC: url_parser::URL::parse  (verified byte-for-byte against
/workspace/dataset/test5_executable, GCC 12 -O0, pre-C++11 std::string ABI)
========================================================================

--- 0. DRIVER (test5.cpp) -----------------------------------------------
main(argc, argv):
    if argc < 2: exit(1)                  # NO output at all, not even newlines
    u = URL(argv[1])                       # ctor resets state then calls parse()
    write(scheme_bytes); write("\n")
    write(host_bytes);   write("\n")
    write(decimal_int(port)); write("\n")  # plain ostream<<int: "-1", "0", "65535";
                                           # no '+', no grouping, no padding, no locale effect
    write(path_bytes);   write("\n")
    write(query_bytes);  write("\n")
    exit(0)

Notes on the I/O contract:
  * Exactly 5 '\n'-terminated records are emitted. Fields are raw bytes,
    echoed verbatim; a field containing 0x0A therefore produces MORE than 5
    physical lines. Empty input yields exactly 7 bytes: 0A 0A 2D 31 0A 0A 0A.
  * argv[1] is a NUL-terminated C string, so an embedded 0x00 truncates the
    input before the parser ever sees it (execve/libc artifact, NOT parser logic).
  * argv[2..] are ignored entirely.
  * Exit status is always 0 whenever argv[1] exists. Nothing is ever written to
    stderr. No input can make the process abort, hang, or throw out of main.
  * The process never calls setlocale(), so it runs in the "C" locale no matter
    what LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE say (verified: LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 still folds 'I'->'i',
    and 0xA0 is never whitespace).

--- 1. PARSE -----------------------------------------------------------
All indices are BYTE indices into a length-counted byte string (std::string):
no NUL sensitivity, no UTF-8 awareness, no character classes beyond the ones
spelled out below.

find_byte(s, b)   := smallest i in [0, len(s)) with s[i] == b, else NONE.
                     (forward search from offset 0 -- NOT rfind, NOT
                      find_first_of; the start offset argument is literally 0
                      at every one of the 5 call sites)
find_sub3(s, "://"):= smallest i in [0, len(s)-2] with s[i..i+3) == ":" "/" "/",
                     else NONE.  (forward search from offset 0)
s[a..b)           := bytes a inclusive .. b exclusive
s[a..]            := s[a..len(s))   (implemented as substr(a, npos))

parse(url):
    # ---- reset (every field, unconditionally) ----
    scheme = ""; userinfo = ""; host = ""; port = -1
    path = "";  query = "";  fragment = ""
    rest = url                       # working copy

    # ---- STEP 1: FRAGMENT. Highest precedence. Runs on the RAW input,
    #              BEFORE query split, BEFORE scheme detection. ----
    hp = find_byte(rest, 0x23 '#')
    if hp != NONE:
        fragment = rest[hp+1 ..]     # stored but NEVER printed by the driver
        rest     = rest[0 .. hp)     # '#' itself is dropped
    # => no byte at or after the first '#' can ever reach scheme/host/port/path/query.
    # => a '#' before a "://" destroys scheme AND host.
    # => only the FIRST '#' matters; later '#'s are already inside the discard.

    # ---- STEP 2: QUERY. Second precedence. Runs on the fragment-stripped
    #              string, over its WHOLE length, BEFORE scheme detection. ----
    qp = find_byte(rest, 0x3F '?')
    if qp != NONE:
        query = rest[qp+1 ..]        # to end; later '?'s stay inside query
        rest  = rest[0 .. qp)
    # => a '?' after the first '#' produces NO query (it was already discarded).
    # => a '?' before a "://" destroys scheme AND host; the rest of the URL
    #    (including further "://", '@', ':', '/') lands in query UNPARSED.
    # => empty query and absent query are indistinguishable in the 5-line output.

    # ---- STEP 3: SCHEME, keyed on the literal 3-byte sequence "://" ----
    sp = find_sub3(rest, "://")
    if sp == NONE:
        # ***** NO-AUTHORITY BRANCH *****
        path = rest                  # the ENTIRE remainder, verbatim
        # scheme stays "", host stays "", port stays -1
        return                       # nothing else is parsed: ':' '/' '@' inert
    scheme = ascii_lower(rest[0 .. sp))   # may be EMPTY and that is legal
    rest   = rest[sp+3 ..]                # exactly +3 -- only 2 slashes consumed,
                                          # surplus slashes fall through to path
    # ascii_lower is: for each byte b (taken as unsigned char), C-locale tolower.
    # Verified by exhaustive 1..255 sweep: EXACTLY 0x41..0x5A ('A'..'Z') map to
    # 0x61..0x7A ('a'..'z'); every other byte, including 0x40 '@', 0x5B '[',
    # 0x5C '\', 0x60 '`', 0x7B '{', 0x7F, and ALL bytes 0x80..0xFF, is identity.
    # There is NO scheme character-set validation and NO length limit: '/', ':',
    # '@', ' ', TAB, CR, control bytes, digits, punctuation, high bytes all pass.
    # Only the FIRST "://" is the separator; later ones are ordinary bytes.

    # ---- STEP 4: AUTHORITY / PATH split at the FIRST '/' ----
    slash = find_byte(rest, 0x2F '/')
    if slash != NONE:
        authority = rest[0 .. slash)
        path      = rest[slash ..]   # INCLUDES the leading '/'; runs to end of rest
    else:
        authority = rest
        path      = ""               # NO synthesized "/" -- path stays empty
    # '?' and '#' were already removed, so '/' is the ONLY authority terminator.
    # Backslash, ';', ',', space, TAB, CR, NUL-free control bytes, high bytes,
    # '%' escapes: none of them terminate the authority.

    # ---- STEP 5: USERINFO strip at the FIRST '@' of the authority ----
    at = find_byte(authority, 0x40 '@')
    if at != NONE:
        userinfo  = authority[0 .. at)   # stored, never printed
        authority = authority[at+1 ..]   # remainder is NOT re-scanned for '@'
    # FIRST '@', not last (non-RFC): "u@v@w" leaves authority "v@w".
    # Confined to the authority, so an '@' in path or query is an ordinary byte.
    # Runs BEFORE the port colon, so a ':' left of the first '@' is userinfo.

    # ---- STEP 6: HOST / PORT split at the FIRST ':' of what remains ----
    colon = find_byte(authority, 0x3A ':')
    if colon == NONE:
        host = authority             # port stays -1
        return
    host     = authority[0 .. colon) # FIRST ':', not last; no '[' ']' IPv6 logic
    port_str = authority[colon+1 ..] # to END of authority (may contain ':', '@', ...)
    port     = convert_port(port_str)
    if port < 0 or port > 65535:     # signed compare against 65535
        port = -1
    return

--- 2. convert_port: exact semantics -----------------------------------
The binary calls std::stoi(port_str, /*pos=*/nullptr, /*base=*/10), which is
__gnu_cxx::__stoa(&strtol, "stoi", ...), wrapped in a try/catch whose LSDA
action filter resolves to a NULL ttype, i.e. a bare `catch (...)` whose body is
exactly `port_ = -1;`. Both std::invalid_argument and std::out_of_range are
thrown in practice and both are swallowed silently (exit 0, empty stderr).

convert_port(s) -> int:
    i = 0
    # (a) skip a run of leading whitespace. The set is EXACTLY C-locale isspace:
    #     {0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE}.
    #     Verified by exhaustive byte scan; 0xA0 and every other byte are NOT ws.
    while i < len(s) and s[i] in {0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20}: i += 1
    # (b) at most ONE optional sign, immediately after the whitespace run
    neg = false
    if i < len(s) and (s[i]=='+' or s[i]=='-'):
        neg = (s[i]=='-'); i += 1
    # (c) at least one ASCII digit 0x30..0x39 must follow IMMEDIATELY.
    #     No whitespace may follow the sign. Only ASCII digits count -- no
    #     Unicode/fullwidth/Arabic-Indic digits. Base is fixed 10: no octal
    #     interpretation of leading zeros, no 0x/0X/0b prefixes.
    if i >= len(s) or not (0x30 <= s[i] <= 0x39):
        return SENTINEL_FAIL                 # -> invalid_argument -> caught -> -1
    # (d) consume the maximal run of ASCII digits; STOP at the first non-digit
    #     and silently IGNORE every remaining byte (prefix parse, no
    #     whole-string-consumed check).
    mag = 0 (arbitrary precision)
    while i < len(s) and 0x30 <= s[i] <= 0x39:
        mag = mag*10 + (s[i]-0x30); i += 1
    v = neg ? -mag : +mag
    # (e) strtol overflow: if v does not fit in i64 -> ERANGE -> out_of_range -> -1
    if v < -2^63 or v > 2^63-1: return SENTINEL_FAIL
    # (f) long->int narrowing check: if v does not fit in i32 -> out_of_range -> -1
    if v < -2^31 or v > 2^31-1:  return SENTINEL_FAIL
    return v as i32
    # SENTINEL_FAIL is caught and mapped to -1 by the caller.

Simplification that is observationally IDENTICAL (recommended for a port):
    parse the prefix as above into an arbitrary-precision signed integer;
    if no digit was consumed -> -1;
    else if value is in 0..=65535 -> value;
    else -> -1.
Because every value that would throw (|v| > INT_MAX) is also outside 0..65535,
and because the explicit range check runs after the conversion, all failure
modes collapse onto the single sentinel -1.

CRITICAL corner: "-0" (and " -0", "-00") parses to 0, passes the >=0 check, and
yields port 0. A naive "reject if the string starts with '-'" shortcut is WRONG.
"-1" yields -1 only because the range check rejects it -- it is indistinguishable
from the absent-port sentinel.

--- 3. THINGS THAT DO NOT HAPPEN (all verified in the binary) ----------
  * No default/implicit port for ANY scheme. There is no "http"/"https" string
    literal anywhere in the binary and no scheme->port table; 65535 is the only
    port-related numeric constant. Every schemeless-port URL prints -1.
  * No percent-decoding anywhere. "%23", "%3F", "%2F", "%40", "%3A", "%20",
    lone "%", malformed "%zz" all pass through literally and never act as
    delimiters.
  * No whitespace trimming. A trim() function exists in the binary but is never
    called from any code path.
  * No path normalization. normalize()/normalize_case()/normalize_path()/
    normalize_query() exist but the constructor never calls them: ".", "..",
    empty segments and duplicate slashes are preserved byte-for-byte.
  * No validation. is_scheme_valid(), is_host_valid(), is_port_valid() and
    split_path() exist but are never called. Parsing never fails.
  * No host lowercasing, no IDN/punycode processing, no UTF-8 validation.
    Only the scheme is case-folded.
  * No IPv6 bracket handling: '[' and ']' are ordinary host bytes.
  * No length limits: schemes/hosts/paths/queries/port strings of 100k+ bytes
    round-trip exactly (only the kernel MAX_ARG_STRLEN ~131072 stops argv).
  * The authority-end scan is find('/'), not find_first_of("/?#") -- behaviorally
    indistinguishable here because '?' and '#' were already removed.


CANDIDATE RULES:
- OUTPUT SHAPE: with argv[1] present, exactly 5 '\n'-terminated records are written to stdout in the order scheme, host, port, path, query; exit status is 0 and stderr is always empty. With argc<2 the driver writes nothing at all and exits 1.
- Fields are raw byte strings echoed verbatim, so a field containing 0x0A yields more than 5 physical lines (e.g. 'http://a<LF>b.com' prints 6 lines).
- port() is printed by plain ostream<<int: '-1' for the sentinel, '0'..'65535' otherwise; never a '+', never thousands grouping, never padding. Locale has no effect (the program never calls setlocale, so it stays in the C locale even under LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8).
- PRECEDENCE (absolute, never revisited): (1) truncate at first '#'; (2) split query at first '?'; (3) find first "://"; (4) split authority/path at first '/'; (5) strip through first '@' in authority; (6) split host/port at first ':' in authority.
- STEP 1 fragment: everything from the FIRST 0x23 '#' to end of the RAW input is discarded before any other parsing. No byte at or after that '#' can appear in any of the 5 fields. Only the first '#' matters.
- A '#' occurring before a "://" destroys scheme AND host: 'ht#tp://a.com' -> ''/''/-1/'ht'/''.
- STEP 2 query: query = everything after the FIRST 0x3F '?' of the fragment-stripped string, to its end. The search spans the whole string, not just the path region.
- Because '#' is cut first, a '?' that appears after the first '#' produces NO query. Discriminator: 'a.com#f?q=1' -> query '' (not 'q=1').
- Only the first '?' is a delimiter; later '?' bytes are ordinary query content ('http://a.com/p?a=1?b=2' -> query 'a=1?b=2').
- A '?' before a "://" destroys scheme AND host; the remainder lands in query completely unparsed, including further "://", '@', ':' and '/'.
- Empty query and absent query are indistinguishable (both print an empty line 5). Same for empty vs absent fragment.
- STEP 3 scheme: the one and only trigger for authority parsing is the literal 3-byte sequence 0x3A 0x2F 0x2F "://". A bare ':' is insufficient; '//' without a preceding ':' is insufficient; ':' and '//' must be contiguous.
- If "://" is absent from the fragment- and query-stripped remainder, scheme='', host='', port=-1 and the ENTIRE remainder becomes the path verbatim. In that branch ':', '/', '@' are completely inert.
- scheme = the bytes strictly before the FIRST "://", ASCII-lowercased. Later "://" occurrences are never the separator.
- There is NO scheme character-set validation and no length limit: digits, leading digits, spaces, TAB, CR, control bytes, '/', '\\', ':', '@', '+', '-', '.', '~', '[', '{', DEL and bytes >=0x80 are all accepted as scheme bytes.
- A scheme may end in ':' and may contain ':' ('a:b://c' -> scheme 'a:b'; 'a:://b' -> scheme 'a:'; ':://a' -> scheme ':').
- An EMPTY scheme is legal and distinct from 'no scheme': a leading "://" still runs the authority parse ('://a.com:8080/p?q' -> ''/'a.com'/8080/'/p'/'q'), whereas a string with no "://" puts everything in path.
- Case folding is EXACTLY bytes 0x41..0x5A -> 0x61..0x7A, applied only to the scheme. Verified by exhaustive 1..255 byte sweep: 0x40 '@', 0x5B '[', 0x5C '\\', 0x60 '`', 0x7B '{', 0x7F and every byte 0x80..0xFF are left identical. Implementation is C-locale tolower on unsigned char.
- Host, path and query preserve case and bytes exactly; they are never lowercased, decoded, normalized or trimmed.
- The remainder-parse resumes at exactly (index of first "://") + 3. Only two slashes are consumed, so surplus slashes fall into the path with an empty host ('http:///a' -> host '', path '/a'; 'a://///b' -> host '', path '///b').
- STEP 4 authority/path: the authority ends at the FIRST 0x2F '/' after the separator; path = that '/' through the end of the (fragment/query-stripped) string, leading '/' INCLUDED. If no '/' exists the path is EMPTY -- no default '/' is synthesized.
- Exactly two bytes can terminate a path, and both do so in earlier steps: '?' and '#'. A byte sweep of 1..126 inside a path showed every other byte -- including ':', '@', '\\', ';', '%', '+', '&', '=', space, TAB, CR, DEL -- is retained verbatim.
- STEP 5 userinfo: if the authority contains 0x40 '@', everything up to and including the FIRST '@' is discarded. It is find('@'), not rfind('@'), and the remainder is not re-scanned: 'http://a@b@c' -> host 'b@c'.
- The '@' search is confined to the authority (before the first '/', and '?'/'#' are already gone), so an '@' in path or query never triggers userinfo stripping.
- Userinfo stripping runs BEFORE the port colon is located, so a ':' left of the first '@' is never a port ('http://user:80@a.com' -> port -1) and the port comes from the post-'@' text ('http://a.com:80@b.com:90' -> host 'b.com', port 90).
- STEP 6 host/port: host = authority bytes before the FIRST 0x3A ':'; port string = everything after that ':' to the end of the authority. It is find(':'), not rfind(':'): 'http://a.com:80:90' -> host 'a.com', port 80.
- No IPv6 bracket handling whatsoever: 'http://[::1]:8080' -> host '[', port -1. '[' and ']' are ordinary bytes ('http://[a]:80' -> host '[a]', port 80).
- An empty host is fine and is not an error: 'http://' , 'http://:' , 'http://@' , 'http://a.com@' , 'http://:8080' all parse with host ''.
- PORT CONVERSION is a std::stoi/strtol-style base-10 PREFIX parse: optional run of C-locale whitespace {0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20}, then at most ONE '+' or '-', then one or more ASCII digits; parsing stops at the first non-digit and ALL trailing bytes are silently ignored.
- Whitespace may precede the sign but NOT follow it: ' +80' -> 80, but '+ 80' -> -1, '- 80' -> -1, '++80' -> -1, '-+80' -> -1, bare '+' or '-' -> -1.
- At least one ASCII digit is required; otherwise -1. Only ASCII 0x30..0x39 count -- Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits are rejected. Radix is fixed 10: '080'->80, '0777'->777, '0x50'->0, '0X50'->0, '0b11'->0.
- After conversion an explicit range check accepts only 0 <= v <= 65535; anything else becomes -1. There is NO clamping, NO wraparound, NO uint16 truncation and NO (int) narrowing of a wider result: 65536 -> -1 (not 0), 65616 -> -1 (not 80), 4294967296 -> -1 (not 0), 2147483647 -> -1 (not 65535).
- Negative zero is ACCEPTED: '-0', '-00', ' -0' all yield port 0. Every other negative magnitude yields -1. Do not shortcut on a leading '-'.
- Out-of-int-range and non-numeric port strings throw std::out_of_range / std::invalid_argument inside std::stoi; a bare catch(...) swallows them and assigns -1. Exit status stays 0 and stderr stays empty (100000-digit ports included).
- -1 is a single overloaded sentinel: no ':' in the authority, empty port string, whitespace-only port string, no leading digit, negative value, and out-of-range value are all indistinguishable from port() alone. Since valid ports are 0..65535, -1 is never a genuine port.
- A bad port never poisons the other fields: the host is still truncated at the colon and path/query are still extracted ('http://a.com:abc/p?q=1' -> http/a.com/-1//p/q=1).
- There are NO default ports for any scheme. 25+ schemes probed (http, https, ftp, file, ws, wss, ssh, ldap, redis, mongodb, ...) all print -1 when no explicit port is given. The binary contains no 'http'/'https' literal and no scheme->port table; 65535 is the only port constant.
- No scheme is special-cased at all: 'file:///etc/passwd' -> file/''/-1//etc/passwd/''. No scheme whitelist ('httpx://a.com' parses). Opaque URIs without "://" (mailto:, urn:, tel:, javascript:, data:, about:, 'C:\\path\\file') land wholly in path.
- Protocol-relative '//host/path' is NOT supported -- it becomes pure path.
- No percent-decoding anywhere: '%23', '%3F', '%2F', '%40', '%3A', '%20', a lone '%' and malformed '%zz' pass through literally and never act as delimiters.
- No whitespace trimming anywhere: leading spaces become part of the scheme, interior/trailing spaces stay in host, path and query. (A trim() function exists in the binary but is never called.)
- No path normalization: '.', '..', empty segments and duplicate slashes are preserved byte-for-byte. (normalize()/normalize_path() exist but the constructor never calls them.)
- No host validation, no IDN/punycode decoding, no UTF-8 validation: empty labels, leading/trailing dots and dashes, 300-char labels, raw 0xFF bytes and UTF-8 sequences all pass through unchanged.
- No length limits: 50000-byte schemes, 300-byte hosts, 5000-byte paths, 1200-byte queries, 100000-digit port strings all work with exit 0. The only ceiling is the kernel's MAX_ARG_STRLEN (~131072 bytes) on argv, which is not a parser limit.
- Parsing never fails and never throws out of the constructor. Every input tested -- including '', ':', '//', '///', '#', '?', '@', '://' and raw non-UTF-8 bytes -- produced 5 records and exit 0.
- An embedded 0x00 in argv truncates the string at the C-string level before the parser runs; this is an execve/libc artifact, not parser behaviour, and internal parsing is length-based (std::string), not NUL-terminated.
- Only argv[1] is read; argv[2..] are ignored.

Report a list of concrete divergences (input, what the spec predicts, what the binary really does)
and any newly discovered rules. If you find no divergence in your lens after a genuinely thorough
attack, say so explicitly and list the inputs that confirmed the spec.

MULTIBYTE: all scanning is byte-level with zero encoding awareness. Decisive proof: a delimiter byte occurring as the SECOND byte of a two-byte sequence (Shift-JIS style, where 0x40/0x3A/0x2F/0x3F/0x23 are legal trail bytes) is fully honoured as a delimiter, splitting the multibyte character in half.
rules.evidence: 'http://h\x82\x40x:80' -> http | x | 80 | '' | ''  (the 0x40 acted as userinfo '@').  'http://h\x83\x3Ax:80' -> http | h\x83 | -1 | '' | ''  (0x3A acted as port colon).  'http://h\x84\x2Fx:80' -> http | h\x84 | -1 | /x:80 | ''.  'http://h\x85\x3Fx:80' -> http | h\x85 | -1 | '' | x:80.  'http://h\x86\x23x:80' -> http | h\x86 | -1 | '' | ''.

rules.rule: Conversely, Unicode LOOKALIKES of the delimiters never delimit (no normalization, no confusable folding): FF1A fullwidth colon, FF0F fullwidth solidus, FF20 fullwidth commercial at, FF1F, FF03, FF3B/FF3D fullwidth brackets, U+2044 fraction slash, U+2215 division slash, U+FE55, U+A789 are all inert bytes.
rules.evidence: 'http\xEF\xBC\x9A\xEF\xBC\x8F\xEF\xBC\x8Fh.com' -> '' | '' | -1 | http\xEF\xBC\x9A\xEF\xBC\x8F\xEF\xBC\x8Fh.com | ''  (no "://" -> all path).  'http://u\xEF\xBC\xA0h.com:80' -> http | u\xEF\xBC\xA0h.com | 80 | '' | ''  (fullwidth '@' did NOT strip userinfo).  'http://\xEF\xBC\xBB::1\xEF\xBC\xBD:8080' -> http | \xEF\xBC\xBB | -1 | '' | ''.

rules.rule: Overlong / invalid UTF-8 encodings of delimiters are NOT decoded, so they cannot forge a "://" separator.
rules.evidence: 'http:\xC0\xAF\xC0\xAFh.com' (overlong '/' twice) -> '' | '' | -1 | http:\xC0\xAF\xC0\xAFh.com | ''.  'http\xC0\xBA//h.com' (overlong ':') -> '' | '' | -1 | http\xC0\xBA//h.com | ''.

rules.rule: Scheme case folding is EXACTLY 0x41..0x5A -> 0x61..0x7A and nothing else, verified by exhaustive sweep of every byte 0x01..0xFF in three scheme positions. In particular no Latin-1 high-byte pair (0xC0..0xDE / 0xE0..0xFE) is folded, and no UTF-8 uppercase letter (Latin-1 supplement, Greek, Cyrillic, fullwidth, Deseret, KELVIN SIGN U+212A, Turkish dotted I U+0130) is folded.
rules.evidence: 3825-input sweep (templates 'a<b>b://...', '<b>://...', 'A<b>Z://H.CoM:80/P?Q' for b=0x01..0xFF) matched the ASCII-only model on all 255 bytes.  'HTTP\xC9\xD6://h:80' -> http\xC9\xD6 | h | 80 | '' | ''  (Latin-1 E-acute/O-uml NOT folded to \xE9\xF6).  'HTTP\xC3\x89://h:80' -> http\xC3\x89 | h | 80 | '' | ''.  '\xE2\x84\xAA://h' -> \xE2\x84\xAA | h | -1 | '' | ''.  '\xC4\xB0://h' -> \xC4\xB0 | h | -1 | '' | ''.  '\xEF\xBC\xA1\xEF\xBC\xA2://h' -> \xEF\xBC\xA1\xEF\xBC\xA2 | h | -1 | '' | ''.  '\xD0\x90\xD0\x91://h' -> \xD0\x90\xD0\x91 | h | -1 | '' | ''.

rules.rule: Host / path / query are never case-folded even inside brackets, and a leading UTF-8 BOM is not stripped — it becomes part of the scheme verbatim.
rules.evidence: 'http://[ABC]:80' -> http | [ABC] | 80 | '' | ''.  'HTTP://[ABCDEF]' -> http | [ABCDEF] | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://EXAMPLE.COM:80/PATH?Q=A' -> http | EXAMPLE.COM | 80 | /PATH | Q=A.  '\xEF\xBB\xBFhttp://h.com:80/p?q' -> \xEF\xBB\xBFhttp | h.com | 80 | /p | q  (scheme is 7 bytes).

rules.rule: PORT whitespace skipping is exactly the 6 C-locale ASCII bytes {09,0A,0B,0C,0D,20}; no multibyte 'space' qualifies. Verified by exhaustive byte sweep at 'http://h:<b>80' for b=0x01..0xFF plus explicit UTF-8 space characters.
rules.evidence: 'http://h.com:\xC2\xA080' (U+00A0 NBSP) -> http | h.com | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://h.com:\xE3\x80\x8080' (U+3000) -> http | h.com | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://h.com:\xE1\x9A\x8080' (U+1680) -> -1.  'http://u@h.com:\xA080' -> -1.  Positive control 'http://u@h.com: \x09\x0D\x0A+80' -> http | h.com | 80 | '' | ''.  Trailing high bytes are ignored: 'http://h.com:80\xC2\xA0' -> 80; 'http://[::1]:80\xFF' -> -1 (bracket case, colon at index 1).

rules.rule: PORT digits are exactly ASCII 0x30..0x39 and the sign exactly ASCII '+'/'-'; no Unicode digit or Unicode sign is accepted.
rules.evidence: 'http://h:\xD9\xA8\xD9\xA0' (Arabic-Indic 8,0) -> http | h | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://h:\xEF\xBC\x98\xEF\xBC\x90' (fullwidth 8,0) -> -1.  'http://h:\xE0\xA5\xA8\xE0\xA5\xA6' (Devanagari) -> -1.  'http://h:\xE2\x88\x9280' (U+2212 MINUS SIGN then 80) -> -1.  'http://h:\xEF\xBC\x8B80' (U+FF0B FULLWIDTH PLUS) -> -1.  'http://h:\xFF80' -> -1.  Positive control 'http://[1]:+80' -> 80 and 'http://[1]:-0' -> 0.

rules.rule: High-bit and non-UTF-8 bytes are transported byte-for-byte through every one of the 5 fields, including lone continuation bytes, 0xFE/0xFF, truncated sequences, out-of-range F4/F5 leads, and CESU-8 surrogate pairs. Exit is always 0 and stderr always empty (0 bytes).
rules.evidence: 'HTTP\xC3\x89://[\xFF::1]:65535/\xFF?\xFF' -> http\xC3\x89 | [\xFF | -1 | /\xFF | \xFF, exit=0, stderr=0 bytes.  'http://\xFF\xFE@[\xFF]:0' -> http | [\xFF] | 0 | '' | ''.  'http://\xC3\xA9:\xC3\xA8@\xC3\xAA.com:8080/p?q' -> http | \xC3\xAA.com | 8080 | /p | q.  'http://\xFF@\xFF:\xFF' -> http | \xFF | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://\xC3\x89\xC3\x88\xC3\x8A.COM:80/p?q' -> http | \xC3\x89\xC3\x88\xC3\x8A.COM | 80 | /p | q.

rules.rule: A 0x0A inside a high-byte host still simply produces extra physical lines (field echoed verbatim), confirming the raw-byte I/O contract in the multibyte case.
rules.evidence: 'http://\xC3\xA9\x0Ahost\xFF:80/p?q' prints 6 physical lines: 'http' / '\xC3\xA9' / 'host\xFF' / '80' / '/p' / 'q', exit=0, stderr empty.

rules.rule: No length limits in this lens: 60 kB high-byte hosts, 30 k-codepoint UTF-8 hosts and bracket bodies, 25 k-codepoint high-byte schemes, 50 kB high-byte port strings, 30 k '@' runs, 30 k '[' runs and a ~127 kB 0xFE path all parse byte-exactly with exit 0.
rules.evidence: 11-input huge batch (60000x0xFF host; 30000x'\xC3\xA9' host; 20000x'\xC3\xA9' bracket body; 15000x'u\xFF:' userinfo; 25000x'\xC3\x89' scheme; 50000x0xFF port prefix; 50001-digit port; 30000 '@'; 30000 ':'; 30000 '['; 126980x0xFE) -> 0 mismatches vs the reference model.

uncertainties: The spec's causal claim "The process never calls setlocale(), so it runs in the C locale no matter what LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE say (verified: LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 still folds 'I'->'i', and 0xA0 is never whitespace)" is NOT verifiable in this container, and the cited evidence is void. I compiled an oracle (/tmp/loc.c, gcc-12): setlocale(LC_ALL,"tr_TR.UTF-8") returns NULL here — the locale does not load, even though `locale -a` lists it. Only C, POSIX, C.UTF-8 and en_US.utf8 actually load. I then scanned every name from `locale -a` (/tmp/scan.c) for a loadable locale whose byte-level tolower or isspace differs from C: there is none (all report tolower_diffs=0 and isspace={09 0A 0B 0C 0D 20}). So 'no setlocale' and 'setlocale + locale-aware tolower' are observationally IDENTICAL in this environment. The behavioural conclusion (C-locale semantics: only 0x41..0x5A fold, only 6 ASCII bytes are port whitespace) is solid; the mechanism is not testable here.

For the same reason, the spec's implementation attributions inside my lens are unfalsifiable: 'C-locale tolower on unsigned char' vs 'tolower on signed char' vs a hand-rolled `if (c>='A'&&c<='Z') c+=32` are byte-for-byte identical for all 255 bytes (my 3825-input exhaustive scheme sweep matched the pure-ASCII model exactly). Likewise the port whitespace skip cannot be distinguished from a hard-coded {09,0A,0B,0C,0D,20} set. Any of these is a valid implementation.

userinfo and fragment are stored but never printed, so every spec sentence about their CONTENT is unobservable through the 5-line output. Only their delimiting effect is testable. An implementation that discards rather than stores userinfo/fragment is indistinguishable. Concretely: 'userinfo = authority[0..at)' is untestable; 'the remainder is not re-scanned for @' IS testable and confirmed ('http://u@v@w' -> host 'v@w').

The spec is silent on encoding awareness as a stated rule — it only says 'no UTF-8 validation' and 'no IDN/punycode'. I found the stronger, decisive fact worth adding explicitly: delimiter bytes occurring as multibyte TRAIL bytes are honoured, splitting characters in half ('http://h\x82\x40x:80' -> host 'x', port 80). Anyone implementing from the spec on a char/codepoint-oriented string type (e.g. Rust String, Python str, Java String) would get this wrong; the spec should state that all five delimiter searches are over raw bytes.

I did not probe the exact kernel MAX_ARG_STRLEN boundary byte-by-byte. I confirmed a ~127 kB argument (126,980 bytes of 0xFE plus 'http://') works with exit 0, consistent with the spec's ~131072 note, but the precise cutoff and its failure mode (execve E2BIG before the process starts) were not characterised.

0x00 cannot be tested as a parser byte at all — it is truncated by execve/argv before the parser runs (my harness flagged exactly this on 'http://a\x00b'). So the spec's claim that internal parsing is length-based rather than NUL-terminated is unverifiable from the outside; it is consistent with, but not proven by, the observations.
